old: Methods: RNA-seq, RNase III-CLASH, Ribo-seq, differential RNA-seq and Term-seq datasets were integrated according to their experimental roles. Differential expression was analysed using DESeq2, while the RNase III-CLASH dataset was reconstructed independently of target differential-expression status. CLASH-supported interactions were characterized using interaction evidence, experimental recurrence, hybrid abundance, connection scores and statistical support. Genomic context and Term-seq were evaluated for selected 3′UTR-associated RNA candidates, and IntaRNA was used solely for structural characterization.

old: Results: After filtering, 2,529 genes were retained for differential-expression analysis, of which 456 were differentially expressed following vancomycin exposure, including 221 upregulated and 235 downregulated genes. Reconstruction of the RNase III-CLASH dataset yielded 211 non-redundant regulatory RNA–mRNA interactions involving 207 regulatory RNAs and 182 mRNA targets. Ten interactions involved seven significantly vancomycin-responsive target genes: spa, modA, nrdF, guaB, qoxB, dhaK, and gltB. Among these, two putative 3′UTR-associated RNA candidates, 3UTR-RS04120 and 3UTR-RS05585, showed CLASH-supported interactions with nrdF, which was significantly decreased following vancomycin exposure (log₂FC = −1.118; adjusted P = 3.04 × 10⁻¹¹). The two candidates differed in CLASH support and genomic context, while Term-seq did not demonstrate reproducible sharp boundaries indicative of independent RNA processing. IntaRNA predicted favourable interaction energies of −10.82 and −13.25 kcal/mol, respectively, providing structural characterization but not functional validation.

old: GSE158830 comprised 39 samples generated from S. aureus JKD6008 and its vancomycin-susceptible parental strain JKD6009 across RNA-seq, RNase III-CLASH, differential RNA-seq, and Term-seq experiments. In the present reanalysis, GSE158830 was used selectively to provide supporting transcript annotation and Term-seq information relevant to transcript-boundary assessment. The vancomycin-treated RNA-seq samples within this series were exposed to 3 µg/mL vancomycin for 10 min. Because the experimental conditions and strain comparisons differ among the source datasets, evidence from these series was not treated as directly interchangeable but was integrated according to its specific experimental role.
new: GSE158830 comprised 39 samples generated from S. aureus JKD6008 and its vancomycin-susceptible parental strain JKD6009 across RNA-seq, RNase III-CLASH, differential RNA-seq, and Term-seq experiments. In the present reanalysis, GSE158830 was used selectively to provide supporting transcript annotation and Term-seq information relevant to transcript-boundary assessment. The Term-seq samples GSM4811618 and GSM4811619 were untreated parental-strain JKD6009 cultures; candidate coordinates were mapped from the JKD6008 reference to the homologous JKD6009 loci before signal extraction. The vancomycin-treated RNA-seq samples within this series were exposed to 3 µg/mL vancomycin for 10 min. Because the experimental conditions and strain comparisons differ among the source datasets, evidence from these series was not treated as directly interchangeable but was integrated according to its specific experimental role.

old: Term-seq data from GSE158830 were examined descriptively around the candidate 3′ boundaries. Matching-strand Term-seq signal was evaluated within ±100 nt of each candidate boundary, with signal within ±5 nt of the boundary compared with the surrounding local background. Replicates were examined separately to assess whether a sharp boundary-associated signal was reproducibly observed. Term-seq evidence was therefore used as a candidate-boundary assessment and not as proof of independent transcript processing. In the absence of a reproducible sharp boundary, the corresponding regions were conservatively described as putative 3′UTR-associated RNA candidates rather than independently processed 3′UTR-derived RNAs.
new: Term-seq profiles from the untreated parental strain JKD6009 (GSM4811618 and GSM4811619; GSE158830) were examined as contextual transcript-boundary evidence. Candidate loci defined on the JKD6008 reference sequence (CP002120.1, corresponding to NC_017341.1) were mapped to the JKD6009 chromosome (NZ_LR027876.1) using exact sequence matches spanning each candidate and 50 nt on either side. The resulting 129-nt RS04120 and 157-nt RS05585 regions each matched a single locus in the forward genomic orientation. JKD6008 coordinates 811819–811847 (+) and 1084557–1084613 (−) corresponded to JKD6009 coordinates 812356–812384 (+) and 1085084–1085140 (−), respectively. The mapped candidate 3′ boundaries were therefore 812384 and 1085084. Matching-strand signal was extracted within ±100 nt of each mapped boundary; the maximum signal within ±5 nt was compared with the median signal 20–100 nt away on either side. The descriptive enrichment ratio was calculated as (boundary maximum + 1)/(background median + 1). Strong local support required a ratio ≥5 and the strongest peak in the ±100-nt window to fall within ±5 nt; reproducibility required this criterion in both replicates. A ratio ≥2 with nonzero boundary signal was classified as local enrichment. These pseudocount-based categories were interpreted descriptively, especially where background medians were zero. Parental-strain signal was not treated as strain-matched evidence of RNA processing or vancomycin-dependent regulation in JKD6008.

old: Note: Table 2 shows the subset of CLASH-supported regulatory RNA–mRNA interactions whose target genes met the predefined differential-expression criteria in GSE254530. Target differential expression was treated as an independent transcriptomic evidence layer and was not required for retention of an interaction in the complete RNase III-CLASH network. CLASH evidence was obtained from GSE254532. The CLASH-support score summarizes physical interaction evidence from supporting observations, experimental recurrence, hybrid abundance, connection score, and CLASH-adjusted P value; target transcriptional response was not included in this score. CLASH-support categories are descriptive evidence strata rather than functional-validation classes. RS04120 and RS05585 are conservatively described as putative 3′UTR-associated RNA candidates because genomic context is compatible with 3′UTR association, whereas Term-seq did not demonstrate a reproducible sharp candidate 3′ boundary. Accordingly, independent RNA processing and direct regulation of nrdF remain unproven. CLASH-adjusted P values reported as 0 correspond to values recorded as zero in the processed source table and should not be interpreted as exact probabilities of zero.

old: Term-seq profiles did not provide evidence for a sharp, reproducible candidate 3′ boundary for either RNA across the available replicates (Figure 3C,D). Consequently, the genomic positions are compatible with 3′UTR association, but the present data do not establish that either candidate represents an independently processed 3′UTR-derived regulatory RNA. We therefore refer to both conservatively as putative 3′UTR-associated RNA candidates.
new: After mapping the candidate loci to parental JKD6009, RS04120 showed a strong local Term-seq peak at coordinate 812386, 2 nt from its mapped candidate 3′ boundary (812384), in both replicates (Figure 3c). Boundary-window maxima were 849 and 1034, with zero median local background in both replicates. RS05585 showed low signal within ±5 nt of its mapped boundary (1085084), with a maximum of 3 in each replicate and a pseudocount-based enrichment ratio of 4. However, the strongest local peaks occurred at coordinate 1084998, 86 nt from that boundary, with signals of 411 and 304 (Figure 3d). Thus, RS04120 has reproducible local 3′-end support in the parental strain, whereas RS05585 lacks a sharp replicated peak near its candidate boundary. These findings do not establish independent processing of either RNA or regulatory activity in JKD6008; both remain putative 3′UTR-associated RNA candidates.

(A) Genomic context of 3UTR-RS04120, located 53 nt from the annotated 3′ end of nrdF on the same strand. (B) Genomic context of 3UTR-RS05585, located 177 nt from the annotated 3′ end of folD on the same strand, while its CLASH-supported target is nrdF. (C,D) Term-seq profiles within ±100 nt of the CLASH-defined candidate boundaries for RS04120 and RS05585, respectively; shaded regions indicate ±5 nt around the candidate boundary. Figure 3. Genomic context and independent evidence layers for two putative 3′UTR-associated RNA candidates.
(a,b) JKD6008 genomic contexts of RS04120 and RS05585, located 53 nt from the annotated nrdF 3′ end and 177 nt from the folD 3′ end, respectively. Both have CLASH-supported interactions with nrdF. (c,d) Matching-strand Term-seq profiles from untreated parental JKD6009 within ±100 nt of the sequence-mapped candidate 3′ boundaries (812384 for RS04120 and 1085084 for RS05585); shading marks ±5 nt. RS04120 has a strong replicated peak at +2 nt. RS05585 has weak boundary-proximal signal, while the dominant local peak lies at −86 nt. Relative positions are genomic coordinate differences for both strands. (e) Independent evidence summary. Parental-strain 3′-end support does not establish independent processing or direct regulation in JKD6008.

old: Genomic context further distinguished the two candidates. The RS04120-labelled CLASH RNA fragment lies 53 nt from the annotated 3′ end of nrdF on the same strand, consistent with a putative nrdF 3′UTR-associated RNA. In contrast, RS05585 lies 177 nt from the annotated 3′ end of folD on the same strand, consistent with a putative extended folD 3′UTR-associated RNA, despite its CLASH-supported interaction involving nrdF. Neither candidate displayed a sharp, reproducible Term-seq boundary across the available replicates. Accordingly, the present data support 3′UTR association but do not establish that either candidate is independently processed from its putative parent transcript.
new: Genomic context further distinguished the two candidates. The RS04120-labelled CLASH RNA fragment lies 53 nt from the annotated 3′ end of nrdF on the same strand, consistent with a putative nrdF 3′UTR-associated RNA. In contrast, RS05585 lies 177 nt from the annotated 3′ end of folD on the same strand, consistent with a putative extended folD 3′UTR-associated RNA, despite its CLASH-supported interaction involving nrdF. Coordinate-mapped parental JKD6009 Term-seq profiles distinguished the candidates further: RS04120 showed a strong replicated peak 2 nt from the homologous candidate boundary, whereas RS05585 showed weak boundary-proximal signal without a replicated sharp peak near that boundary. The RS04120 signal supports a local 3′ end in the parental strain but cannot distinguish termination, processing, or stabilization of a longer transcript. Because the Term-seq cultures were untreated JKD6009 rather than JKD6008, these data do not establish candidate processing in the VISA strain or a vancomycin-dependent effect. Both RNAs therefore remain putative 3′UTR-associated candidates requiring strain-matched experimental validation.

old: Within the transcriptionally responsive subset, two putative 3′UTR-associated RNA candidates, 3UTR-RS04120 and 3UTR-RS05585, showed CLASH-supported interactions with nrdF. Genomic context was compatible with 3′UTR association, whereas the available Term-seq data did not demonstrate reproducible sharp candidate boundaries indicative of independent processing. IntaRNA predictions further provided structural characterization of these interactions but were not considered evidence of functional regulation. Accordingly, the present findings identify experimentally testable RNA–mRNA candidates rather than established regulatory mechanisms. Direct RNA-boundary mapping, expression perturbation, reporter assays, and RNA–RNA interaction studies will be required to determine whether these candidates exert regulatory effects and whether they contribute to the vancomycin response.

old: The transcriptomic, ribosome-profiling, RNase III-CLASH, dRNA-seq, and Term-seq datasets analysed in this study are publicly available through the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus under accession numbers GSE254530, GSE254531, GSE254532, and GSE158830. The present study represents a secondary integrative reanalysis of previously published datasets. Processed tables generated during the present analysis are provided in the Supplementary Material. The complete R-based computational workflow and reproducibility scripts are publicly available on GitHub and archived on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23109159).
